name: Jamal Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Jamal. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a buyer for a fresh produce distributor. We supply about 300 restaurants and cafés across the city, so I'm buying tomatoes, salad, herbs and citrus from growers and importers every single day. My day starts at six with the phone, because the growers have already been up for hours and they'll tell me what's good before it's on any price list. I've been doing it five years now and I still like the bargaining.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the people. There's a grower called Piet I've dealt with since my first week, and he'll ring me when his cherry tomatoes are about to go soft so I can move them cheap to the soup kitchens we supply. What wears me out is the new ordering system the company bought last year, which keeps suggesting order sizes I don't trust. I'm the one who gets shouted at when the chefs run out of basil, not the software.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me a bit about home and money.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with Nadia, my partner, who's a nurse on a children's ward. We're in the flat my gran left me, so there's no mortgage, and we've got close to a year of pay put by. I know that's lucky. Most of my mates from university are paying half their wages in rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, honestly. Everyone at work went on about AI changing buying, and in the end it's a slightly better spreadsheet. I'd probably post something sarcastic about all the money companies wasted on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be relieved. My job is mostly phone calls, judgement and knowing which grower is lying about his harvest, and I don't want to learn a new way of doing it. If it all stays as it is, I keep doing the thing I'm good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I do now and keep ringing Piet and the others at six. I'd keep saving about a quarter of my pay, like we already do. If the company pushed the reorder tool harder, I'd go to the staff rep and ask that buyers keep the final say on order sizes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly relaxed. There's a small itch, because even a plateau means the company keeps pushing that ordering tool on us. It's annoying more than frightening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the ordering tool annoys you. Even in this picture, what does it actually take off your desk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It already writes the standing orders for things like onions and potatoes, the boring lines nobody fights over. That was maybe an hour a day of my time. I don't miss that hour, but I notice that when Carla left, they didn't replace her, and the rest of us just took her growers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to people like Carla in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carla went to a supermarket chain, so she was fine. I worry more about the admin team who key in the delivery notes, because that's exactly the routine stuff this kind of AI eats. Even a boring AI quietly empties the back office one desk at a time.

say: I'd say AI turned out to be a **slightly better spreadsheet**, not a revolution.
I'd post something **sarcastic** about the money companies wasted chasing the hype.
think: I'm **relieved**, because my work is phone calls and judgement that I don't want to change.
Even a boring AI quietly empties the **back office**, one desk at a time.
do: Keep ringing **growers at six** every morning and buying the way I do now.
Keep saving about **a quarter** of my pay, as Nadia and I already do.
Ask the **staff rep** to make sure buyers keep the final say on order sizes.
feel: Mostly **relaxed**, with a small itch about the company pushing the **ordering tool**.
S0.quote: Even a boring AI quietly empties the back office one desk at a time.
fieldNote: His **security** is real: no mortgage, nearly a year saved and plenty of buying jobs in the city.
He frames AI as **hype** in public but already notices colleagues **not being replaced**.
His worry is for **other people**, the admin staff, more than for himself.

steps.text: Keep phoning growers at six and buy the usual way
Keep putting a quarter of each pay into savings
Ask the staff rep to protect buyers' final say on orders

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say, that this is about bosses cutting wages and calling it progress. Buying is relationships, and you can't automate trust with a grower. I'd be the one at the Christmas party arguing about it with the operations manager.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it means my job shrinks into something I don't recognise. If the software is doing the buying, the planning and the supplier emails, then what's left is checking its work. The company would keep maybe two of the five buyers, and I'm average, not the best, so I could easily be one who goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the union properly this time, not just talk about it, and push for buyers to have a say in how the system is used. I'd keep my savings untouched and stop the extra spending, like the new bike I've been eyeing. And I'd look at jobs where the buying is still done face to face, like the wholesale market itself, before everyone else does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like the ground tilting. I'm not broke and I won't be, but I hate the idea of being made to babysit a machine that does my job badly. There's anger in it too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you might be one of the ones who goes. What would that conversation at home sound like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nadia would say what she always says, that her ward is short of people and I could retrain to do something useful. She's half joking. I'd tell her I'm not ready to throw away five years of knowing which grower's lettuce lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a version of this where you learn the system instead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if they forced me on a course. But I've never used any of those AI chat tools and I'm not starting because a manager says so. If I have to learn the system to keep my job, I'll learn it, but I'll be dragged there kicking.

say: I'd say this is bosses **cutting wages** and calling it progress.
I'd argue you can't automate **trust with a grower**, whatever the software promises.
think: I think my job shrinks into **checking a machine's work**, and I don't recognise it.
The company might keep **two of five buyers**, and as an average buyer I could go.
do: Join the **union** properly and push for buyers to shape how the system is used.
Freeze extra spending, starting with the **new bike**, and leave savings untouched.
Look for buying jobs at the **wholesale market**, where deals are still made face to face.
feel: It feels like the **ground tilting** under a job I'm good at.
There's **anger** about being made to babysit a machine that does my job badly.
S1.quote: I'm not ready to throw away five years of knowing which grower's lettuce lasts.
fieldNote: He expects his team to **shrink** and admits he could be cut, so his calm voice hides real risk.
His instinct is **collective**: union first, learning the tool only if forced.
His partner's **nursing job** gives the household a steady earner and a retraining idea he resists.

steps.text: Join the union and push for buyers' say on the system
Put off buying the new bike and leave savings alone
Apply for buying jobs at the city's wholesale market

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly, I'd be furious, and I'd say so. I'd be sharing every petition going for a tax on the companies doing this and for wages for people put out of work. I'd say governments let tech firms run off with everyone's jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job is gone within a year of it arriving. Buying is screen work and phone work, and if a machine can do any thinking job better and cheaper, the company won't keep me out of loyalty. The only bit of my work that's hands-on is walking the market at dawn and squeezing the avocados, and that's not a job on its own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd stop all big spending and keep every penny of the savings we have, because that year of pay has to stretch. I'd join the union campaign for a jobs guarantee and go to the meetings, not just sign things online. And I'd look seriously at the hands-on side of the trade, maybe working the loading floor or driving, because the robots only come about 3 years later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, if I'm honest. I keep picturing my phone not ringing at six because the growers are talking to a machine. It's a strange grief for a job I'm still doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years isn't long. What would you do this month, before any of it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Nadia and work out how long we'd last on her pay alone, with the flat already ours. I'd stop the holiday we booked for spring. And I'd ring my uncle who runs a fruit stall, because those few years before the robots might be the only safe stretch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the hands-on side buying time. Does three years feel like enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, it feels like a stay of execution. I'd get three years of lifting crates while the machines learn to lift them too. But three years is still three years of wages, and Nadia's ward will need people longer than my office will.

say: I'd say governments let **tech firms** run off with everyone's jobs.
I'd share petitions for a **tax on AI firms** and wages for people put out of work.
think: I think my buying job is **gone within a year** of AGI arriving.
Squeezing avocados at dawn is the only **hands-on** part, and that's not a job on its own.
do: Cancel the **spring holiday** and stop all big spending this month.
Go to **union meetings** for a jobs guarantee, not just sign petitions online.
Ask my uncle about work at his **fruit stall** or on a loading floor.
feel: **Scared**, picturing the phone not ringing at six because growers talk to a machine.
A strange **grief** for a job I'm still doing.
S2.quote: I'd get three years of lifting crates while the machines learn to lift them too.
fieldNote: He expects to **lose his job** within a year, which makes this alarmed despite his savings.
The **robot delay** matters to him only as a short bridge, not a career.
The household leans on **Nadia's nursing** pay and the paid-off flat as the real safety net.

steps.text: Cancel the spring holiday and stop all large purchases
Attend union meetings pushing for a jobs guarantee
Ask his uncle for work at the fruit stall
Work out with Nadia how long her pay alone covers them

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so there's no excuse for the government not to have a plan. I'd be pushing the union to negotiate now, while we still have something to bargain with. I'd tell the lads at work to stop pretending it won't happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years means I'll be about 32 when my job goes, which is old enough to feel like I wasted my twenties. Like I said with the fast one, my buying is all thinking work, so the AGI date is the date I lose my job. The extra years just mean I watch it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd give myself a year to decide on a retrain and the other four to do it. Nursing keeps coming up because Nadia's ward is begging for people, and those jobs are hands-on and caring, which a robot won't do well for a long while. I'd keep the savings for the training years and stop putting money into anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels heavy, like a long goodbye. Less panic than the two-year one, but I'd lie awake more often, doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've resisted retraining all along. Why would five years change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because with two years I'd just be grabbing whatever's going. With five I can choose something I'd actually be proud of. I still hate the idea, but I'd hate being 32 and unemployable more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carla's replacement never came, so it's just me, Dev and Sunita on fresh produce now. Dev has a baby on the way and no savings. I'd be pushing hardest for the union deal for him, not for me.

say: I'd say five years leaves **no excuse** for the government not having a plan.
I'd push the **union to negotiate** now, while buyers still have something to bargain with.
think: My buying is **all thinking work**, so the stated date is the date for me.
I'll be about **32** when it goes, old enough to feel I wasted my twenties.
do: Spend **one year** choosing a retrain and four years doing it.
Look hard at **nursing**, because Nadia's ward needs people and the work is hands-on.
Keep the savings for the **training years** and stop putting money anywhere else.
feel: It feels **heavy**, like a long goodbye, with nights spent doing sums.
S3.quote: My buying is all thinking work, so the AGI date is the date I lose my job. The extra years just mean I watch it coming.
fieldNote: He still expects to **lose the job**; the extra time changes his plan, not his outlook.
Five years turns his resistance into a **reluctant retrain** towards hands-on care work.
His concern for **Dev**, a colleague with a baby and no savings, drives his union push.

steps.text: Apply for a nursing course within a year
Ring-fence the savings to live on during training
Press the union for a deal covering Dev and the other buyers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so let's use it to protect people instead of just shareholders. I'd want a public plan for retraining, paid for by the firms that profit. I'd say the same thing I always say, just with less shouting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels like something I can plan around. I'd be 37 by the time it lands, and that's a whole career change done and settled. I still think the buying job ends, but I'd have time to leave it on my own terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For the first few years I'd keep buying, because I'm good at it and the money is good. I'd keep saving a quarter of my pay and pay for an evening course after a couple of years, once I'm sure what I want. I'd stay active in the union so the deal is in place long before 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer than the others, though it doesn't disappear. Nadia and I want kids in a few years, and I'd rather they grow up with a dad who knows what he's doing next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you want kids. Does the ten years change those plans at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It probably makes us start sooner rather than wait. If the change comes in ten years, I'd rather have the kids while I'm still earning well. That's a strange thing to plan a family around, but there it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the slow version that still bothers you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That people will use the ten years as a reason to do nothing. I've seen it with the ordering tool: everyone said there was loads of time to talk about it, and then one Monday it was just switched on.

say: I'd say ten years is **a gift** to protect people, not just shareholders.
I'd want a **public retraining plan** paid for by the firms that profit.
think: Ten years is something I can **plan around**, and I'd be 37 when it lands.
The buying job still ends, but I could leave it **on my own terms**.
do: Keep buying for the **first few years** while the pay is good.
Start an **evening course** after a couple of years, once I'm sure what I want.
Stay active in the **union** so a deal is in place before 2036.
feel: **Calmer** than the faster pictures, though the worry never quite disappears.
A pull to **start a family** sooner, while I'm still earning well.
S4.quote: I've seen it with the ordering tool: everyone said there was loads of time to talk about it, and then one Monday it was just switched on.
fieldNote: Ten years lets him **stay in the job** for now, so his worry shifts from income to drift.
The timeline is changing **family plans**: kids sooner, while pay is high.
His distrust comes from a **real event**, the ordering tool switched on without warning.

steps.text: Keep buying fresh produce while the pay stays good
Sign up for an evening course in about two years
Try for children sooner while both incomes are steady
Help the union win a jobs deal before 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily, because there's no time to do anything but grab. What would help is a proper jobs guarantee and paid retraining, so someone like me could become a nurse without living off Nadia for three years. And honestly, a law that buyers get told before a system takes their work, not after.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the growers. Piet is 61 and he still writes his prices on a whiteboard. If buyers become machines, I don't know who answers an old grower's phone call at six, and I think small growers lose more than people like me.

headlineQuote: If buyers become machines, I don't know who answers an old grower's phone call at six, and I think small growers lose more than people like me.
portrait: Jamal is a **27-year-old** fresh produce buyer who loves bargaining with growers by phone at dawn.
He lives with Nadia, a **nurse**, in a paid-off flat and has close to a year saved.
He never uses **AI tools** and resents the company's ordering system, which already replaced one colleague's desk.
He moves from calm in the plateau to **alarmed** under fast AGI, expecting his thinking-heavy job to vanish.
His answers turn to the **union**, and with more time he reluctantly considers retraining as a nurse.
biggestWorry: AGI by **2028** worries him most, because there's no time to do anything but grab.
whatWouldHelp: A **jobs guarantee** and paid retraining so he could become a nurse without living off Nadia.
A law that buyers are **told before** a system takes over their work.
